issues.legal_issue: An appeal does not abate when substitution is sought within thirty days after the appellant learns of the respondent’s death and the appellant lacked earlier notice of the death.
material_facts: The respondent died while the appeal was pending.
The appellant’s counsel did not know of the death until learning of it during service efforts.
The appellant applied to substitute the respondent’s legal representatives within thirty days of learning of the death.
issues.conclusion: The appeal had not abated, and the legal representatives were ordered to be substituted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Order 22 Rules 4 and 10A of the Code of Civil Procedure, a pleader who learns of a party’s death must inform the court, which gives notice to the other party; where the appellant lacked knowledge and applied within thirty days of learning of the death, the appeal does not abate.

predicates.pending_appeal: An appeal was pending when a respondent died.
predicates.counsel_unaware_of_death: The appellant’s counsel did not know of the respondent’s death until later notice or service efforts disclosed it.
predicates.substitution_sought_within_30_days_of_kn: The appellant applied to substitute the deceased respondent’s legal representatives within thirty days after learning of the death.

issues.definition: When an appeal is pending, counsel was unaware of the respondent’s death, and substitution is sought within thirty days of learning of it, the appeal does not abate and the legal representatives are substituted.

issues.legal_issue: Statutory compensation benefits introduced by a later amendment are unavailable for an acquisition where possession and the original award predate the amendment’s extension to that acquisition regime.
material_facts: Land was acquired under a state urban improvement statute, and possession was taken before the central amendment was extended to acquisitions under that statute.
The original compensation award was made before that extension.
The state statute provided for interest at six per cent from the date possession was taken but did not itself provide for solatium or the other additional benefits at issue.
A court later awarded the additional benefits under the amended central land acquisition law.
issues.conclusion: The later award of solatium, additional amount, and enhanced statutory interest under the amended central law was not authorized; liability was to be recomputed under the governing state statute, including interest at six per cent from the date possession was taken.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 52 and 60A of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959, as amended by the Rajasthan Amendment Act 29 of 1987, governed the extension and transition of the Central Land Acquisition Act, 1894, as amended by Act 68 of 1984. The court relied on Union of India v. Raghubir Singh, K.S. Paripoornan (II) v. State of Kerala, and Umed Industries and Land Development Co. v. State of Rajasthan in explaining the temporal limits on benefits under Sections 23(1-A), 23(2), and 28; the state statute’s applicable interest provision remained the basis for six per cent interest.

predicates.land_acquisition_proceeding: The proceeding concerns compensation for land acquired under a statutory acquisition regime.
predicates.possession_before_extension: Possession of the acquired land was taken before the later amendment was extended to that acquisition regime.
predicates.original_award_before_extension: The original compensation award was made before the later amendment was extended to that acquisition regime.

issues.definition: For a land acquisition proceeding in which possession and the original award predate the amendment’s extension, the later statutory benefits are unavailable and liability is determined under the law governing the acquisition.

issues.legal_issue: A decree awarding benefits beyond the court’s jurisdiction may be challenged as a nullity in execution even after the decree has become final.
material_facts: The governing acquisition statute did not authorize the additional benefits awarded under the amended central law in this case.
The court nevertheless included those benefits in its order.
The appellant objected to their enforcement in execution under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
The lower courts rejected the objection on the ground that the decree had become final.
issues.conclusion: The additional-benefit award was without jurisdiction and could be challenged in execution; the objection was to be determined under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, with restitution considered under Section 144 if warranted.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure, an executing court may consider whether a decree is a nullity. Sushil Kumar Mehta v. Gobind Ram Bohra and Jaipur Development Authority v. Radhey Shyam establish that a decree made without inherent jurisdiction may be challenged at execution; Hiralal Moolchand Doshi v. Barotraman Lal Ranchhoddas distinguishes an erroneous decree from one that is ultra vires the court’s authority. Section 144 permits restitution where appropriate.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce or resist enforcement of a decree in execution.
predicates.decree_awards_relief_beyond_court_jurisd: The decree grants relief the court lacked jurisdiction or authority to grant.

issues.definition: In an execution proceeding, a decree that grants relief beyond the court’s jurisdiction may be challenged as a nullity.

issues.legal_issue: An enhanced compensation valuation that has become final cannot be reopened through execution objections merely because it was reached on an incorrect principle.
material_facts: A court enhanced the compensation valuation for the acquired land.
The appellant allowed that enhanced valuation to become final.
The execution objection concerned the additional statutory benefits, while the appellant accepted the enhanced valuation as binding.
issues.conclusion: The appellant was bound by the final enhanced valuation, although the additional benefits awarded without jurisdiction could be challenged in execution.
issues.legal_principle: A final determination of the compensation valuation is binding and cannot be reopened in execution merely to correct an error in the exercise of jurisdiction; this is distinct from a jurisdictional nullity, which may be challenged in execution under Section 47 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

predicates.execution_proceeding: A party is seeking to enforce or resist enforcement of a decree in execution.
predicates.compensation_valuation_final: The enhanced compensation valuation has become final.
predicates.challenge_seeks_to_reopen_valuation_only: The execution objection seeks to revisit the valuation because of an alleged error rather than because the court lacked jurisdiction to make it.

issues.definition: In execution, a final compensation valuation is not reopened for an alleged error where the challenge does not assert a jurisdictional nullity.
